correct: Part thick grass with a stick and look before you reach in.

wrong.text: Reach bare-handed into a clump of palm fronds to pull out a good one.

wrong.why: Spines, insects and snakes reach bare legs and feet. Wear long sleeves and covered shoes.

wrong.text: Swing the cutlass towards a friend who is holding the frond for you.

wrong.text: Cut all the raffia you can find so the class will not need to come back.

wrong.why: A trip turns it into a serious injury. Walk, and carry it pointing down and away from you.

decisions.prompt: You find a stand of raffia palm on a farm by the road. Nobody is there. What do you do?

options.text: Find the owner and ask before you cut a small sample
options.consequence: The owner agrees, and the plants keep growing for later harvests.

options.text: Cut a small amount quickly and go before anyone comes
options.consequence: This is taking without permission, and you could be stopped and lose the samples.

options.text: Cut the whole frond cluster, since you may not return
options.consequence: You have stripped the plant and damaged the source for the whole community.

decisions.prompt: The cane you collected gives strips of different thickness. What do you do before the bending test?

options.text: Cut the soaked set and the dry set to one size
options.consequence: Thickness is now the same throughout, so any difference comes from soaking.

options.text: Soak the thin strips and keep the thick ones for the dry set
options.consequence: Thin strips bend more easily anyway, so the test no longer shows what soaking does.

options.text: Use the strips as they are and take an average at the end
options.consequence: Thickness changes the result, and averaging cannot remove that from the test.

decisions.prompt: You remember four strips after the first eight have soaked for 20 minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Start the test again with all 12 going in together
options.consequence: All the strips get the same 30 minutes, so the comparison is fair.

options.text: Add the four and take all 12 out at the 30-minute mark
options.consequence: Four strips soak for only 10 minutes, so they crack more and spoil the result.

options.text: Leave those four in for an extra hour to make up for it
options.consequence: Those strips have soaked far longer than the others, so the set is not comparable.

decisions.prompt: The dry strips are cracking on the 2 cm rod. A classmate suggests a change. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the same rod and record each crack as it happens
options.consequence: Same rod, same bend: the dry result can be compared with the soaked one.

options.text: Change to a thicker rod so that fewer dry strips crack
options.consequence: A gentler bend makes dry cane look better than it is, and the comparison fails.

options.text: Stop at six strips, because the result is already clear
options.consequence: Six strips cannot be compared fairly with twelve soaked strips.

observations.prompt: You compare the soaked and dry cane. Which result is what you should expect?

options.text: Many more dry strips crack than soaked strips
Soaked and dry strips crack in about equal numbers
options.why: Then soaking would do nothing, but water softens cane fibres.

options.text: Soaked strips crack more, because water weakens cane
options.why: Soaking makes cane pliable. It does not make it brittle.

options.text: No strips crack at all in either set
options.why: Dry cane is rigid and cracks when bent sharply.

observations.prompt: Which sample is natural and rigid when dry?

options.text: Bamboo
Plastic strapping
options.why: It is synthetic, not natural.

options.text: Raffia
options.why: Raffia is natural but flexible.

options.text: Grass
options.why: Grass is natural but flexible.

numerics.prompt: In a bending test, {c} out of {n} cane strips cracked. What percentage cracked?
{c} out of {n} soaked strips cracked. What percentage passed the test?

faults.scenario: Bola handed in her survey table. Her teacher could not use the bending results. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She wrote only 'palm' for two samples and did not state the part of the plant used.
lines.why: The plant part (leaf, stem, bark) must be stated. It is a common way to lose marks.

lines.text: She labelled a sisal sample as raffia because both are pale fibres.
lines.why: Raffia and sisal are different materials. Check the source before you label.

lines.text: She soaked her strips for different times, whatever was convenient.
lines.why: Soaking time must be the same, or the test is not fair.

lines.text: She labelled each sample as she collected it.
lines.why: Labelling at once stops samples being mixed up.

lines.text: She wrote down each result straight after the bend.
lines.why: Recording at once is correct practice.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for carrying out the bending test fairly.
written.explainPrompt: Why must all the strips in the bending test be the same size and soak for the same time?
written.explainGuide: Thickness and soaking time both change how easily cane bends. If only one thing differs between the two sets, namely wet or dry, then the difference in cracking is caused by soaking. This makes it a fair test.

board: Label each sample where you find it

correct: Use a dye pot and spoon kept only for dyeing, never for food.
Lift the pot off the heat with a helper and thick, dry cloths.

wrong.text: Stir the dye with a spoon from the home kitchen and take it back afterwards.
wrong.why: Dye can poison food. Keep dye tools only for dyeing.

wrong.text: Put preservative into an empty water bottle with no label.
wrong.why: Someone may drink it. Keep it in a labelled container, away from food and children.

wrong.text: Pull the hot raffia out of the bath with bare hands to check the colour.
wrong.why: Hot dye scalds and stains skin. Wear gloves and use a stick.

wrong.text: Split the cane towards your chest so you can see the line better.
wrong.why: A slipping blade goes into you. Always split away from your body.

wrong.text: Pour the spent dye bath into the stream behind the school.
wrong.why: It pollutes water that people and animals use. Dispose of it as your teacher directs.

wrong.text: Leave the dye simmering alone while you go for lunch.
wrong.why: A pot left on the heat can boil over or dry out. Someone must stay and watch it.

distractors.name: Rapping iron
distractors.why: It packs a finished weave down. Nothing is woven in this job.

distractors.name: Household bleach
distractors.why: It strips colour and weakens fibres. It is not part of this dye method.

distractors.name: Clear varnish

distractors.name: Tapestry needle
distractors.why: Stitching comes later. Here the material is only being prepared.

distractors.name: Try square

decisions.prompt: Your split raffia strands vary between thin and wide. What do you do?

options.text: Split the wide ones down to match the others
options.consequence: An even width weaves more neatly and takes dye more evenly.

options.text: Keep them as they are, since the weave will hide it
options.consequence: Uneven strands show as a rough, irregular surface in the finished work.

options.text: Sort out and throw away all the thin strands
options.consequence: You waste good material, and the wide strands still need splitting.

decisions.prompt: Part way through the simmer, some raffia floats above the dye. What do you do?

options.text: Press it under with a stick and keep stirring
options.consequence: All the raffia stays under the liquor, so the colour comes out even.

options.text: Leave it, as the colour will spread along the strand
options.consequence: The exposed part takes less dye and comes out patchy.

options.text: Turn the heat right up so that the dye reaches it
options.consequence: Fierce boiling does not cover the raffia, and the strands get tangled.

decisions.prompt: The raffia is rinsed. It is a bright, hot afternoon. Where do you dry it?

options.text: On the drying line in an airy, shaded place
options.consequence: The colour stays bright and the raffia dries without fading.

options.text: On the line in full sun, because it will dry faster
options.consequence: Strong sun fades the dye, which is the commonest mistake in this job.

options.text: Folded in a closed bag so that the dust stays off
options.consequence: It stays damp in the bag and goes mouldy.

decisions.prompt: The hanks feel dry outside but slightly damp at the centre. What do you do?

options.text: Leave them to dry fully before putting them away
options.consequence: They store safely without mould or rot.

options.text: Store them now and spray them with perfume
options.consequence: Scent does nothing for damp. Mould still grows inside the hank.

options.text: Tie them more tightly so the damp is squeezed out
options.consequence: Tight hanks dry more slowly, and mould grows at the centre.

observations.prompt: Two lots of raffia were dyed in one bath. One was dried in the sun, one in the shade. What do you see?

options.text: The shade-dried raffia is brighter
The sun-dried raffia is brighter
options.why: Strong sunlight fades dye. It does not brighten it.

options.text: Both look exactly the same
options.why: Sun drying fades the colour.

options.text: The shade-dried raffia has lost its colour
options.why: Shade protects colour.

observations.prompt: You open a store and the hanks smell musty, with grey spots. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: They were put away damp
They were dyed with too much dye
options.why: Excess dye does not produce grey spots and a musty smell.

options.text: They were dried in the shade
options.why: Shade drying is correct. Storing damp material causes mould.

options.text: The store has too much air moving through it
options.why: Good ventilation prevents mould.

numerics.prompt: You will dye {m} g of raffia at a liquor ratio of 1:30. How many litres of water do you need?
numerics.working: Water = {m} × 30 g. 1,000 g of water is 1 litre, so that is {answer} litres.

numerics.prompt: Dye is used at {p}% of the weight of the raffia. How many grams of dye do you need for {m} g of raffia?

faults.scenario: Musa's dyed raffia came out pale and streaky, and a month later his hanks were mouldy. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He dried the dyed raffia on a sunny wall for the whole afternoon.
lines.why: Strong sun fades dyed raffia. Dry it in the shade.

lines.text: He stored the hanks in a box while they were still damp inside.
lines.why: Damp material goes mouldy. Dry it fully first.

lines.text: He guessed the amount of dye instead of weighing the raffia.
lines.why: The dye is a percentage of the dry weight, so the raffia must be weighed.

lines.text: He wetted the raffia before putting it into the dye.
lines.why: This helps the dye take evenly. It is correct.

lines.text: He rinsed the raffia after dyeing.
lines.why: Rinsing removes loose dye. It is correct.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for dyeing and storing raffia.
written.explainPrompt: Why should dyed raffia be dried in the shade and stored only when fully dry?
written.explainGuide: Strong sunlight fades the dye, so shade keeps the colour bright. Damp material stored away goes mouldy and rots, so it must be thoroughly dry first.

board: Preparing and dyeing raffia and cane
Keep dye tools away from food

correct: Hold the spoke firmly in a block when filing it.
Keep the finished bodkin in a cork or sheath when it is not in use.

wrong.text: Test the point of the new bodkin on your palm.
wrong.why: You can stab yourself. Test it on a scrap of cane.

wrong.text: Carry the bodkin point-up in your shirt pocket.
wrong.why: The point can stab you when you bend. Carry it sheathed or in a tool roll.

wrong.text: Leave the knife open on the desk while you draw it.
wrong.why: An open blade cuts anyone who reaches across. Close or sheathe it.

wrong.text: File the whole spoke to a point so that it is sharp all along.
wrong.why: Only the tip should be sharp. The shank must be smooth so it cannot cut your hand.

wrong.text: Hold the spoke in your bare hand and file towards your fingers.
wrong.why: The file can slip off the end. Secure the spoke and keep your hand behind the work.

wrong.text: Toss the secateurs to a friend across the room.
wrong.why: A flying sharp tool injures people. Hand tools over closed, handle first.

distractors.why: No material is coloured in this job.

distractors.name: Clear varnish

distractors.name: Basket weaving cane
distractors.why: This is a tool drawing job. No weaving is done.

distractors.name: Tapestry frame
distractors.why: It holds woven work. There is nothing to mount here.

distractors.name: Glue gun

decisions.prompt: Your drawing sheet is tight for the secateurs at 1:2. What do you do?

options.text: Keep to 1:2 and arrange the tools again to fit the sheet
options.consequence: Every drawing keeps the stated scale, so sizes can be read off it.

options.text: Shrink the secateurs to about 1:3 without saying so
options.consequence: The drawing is now false, and anyone reading it gets the wrong size.

options.text: Draw it freehand at any size and leave out the scale
options.consequence: A drawing without a stated scale is a common way to lose marks.

decisions.prompt: You need the length of a curved rapping iron. How do you measure it?

options.text: Lay the flexible tape along the curve
options.consequence: This gives the true length, not the shorter straight distance.

options.text: Measure straight between the two ends
options.consequence: The straight line is shorter than the curve, so the drawing comes out wrong.

options.text: Guess it by comparing it with the knife
options.consequence: A guess cannot be used for a scale drawing.

decisions.prompt: Your filed bodkin has a tip but rough file marks along the shank. What do you do?

options.text: Smooth the shank, leaving only the tip sharp
options.consequence: The tool slides into the weave without tearing the cane, and your hand stays safe.

options.text: Leave it, because only the tip touches the cane
options.consequence: Rough shanks tear the material and can cut your hand.

options.text: File the shank sharper to help it go in
options.consequence: A sharp shank is dangerous and tears the cane as it goes in.

decisions.prompt: The work is done. It is a humid day. What do you do with the steel tools?

options.text: Clean them, wipe on a little oil and store them
options.consequence: Oil keeps rust away, so the tools stay smooth and do not tear the materials.

options.text: Rinse them and leave them in the rack to air dry
options.consequence: Water left on steel starts rust, and rusty tools tear material.

options.text: Put them straight into the bag while they are dirty
options.consequence: Dirt holds moisture, so the tools rust and blunt.

observations.prompt: A gap in a cane weave needs opening so that a stake can go in. Which tool does that?

options.text: The bodkin
The rapping iron
options.why: It packs the weave down. It does not pierce.

options.text: The secateurs
options.why: They cut cane.

options.text: The tape measure
options.why: It only measures.

observations.prompt: You try an old rusty bodkin on soft raffia. What do you expect?

options.text: It snags and tears the strands
It slides through better than a clean one
options.why: Rust makes the surface rough, not slippery.

options.text: It colours the raffia evenly

options.text: It makes the raffia stronger

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for making and looking after hand tools.
written.explainPrompt: Why should a drawing of a tool state its scale?
written.explainGuide: The scale links the drawing to the real tool. Anyone can then work out the true size by multiplying the drawn length by the scale, so the drawing is accurate and useful.

board: Keep one scale for all your drawings

correct: Point the needle away from your face when you pull it through.
Sit in good light so that you do not bend close to the needle.

wrong.text: Hold the needle between your lips while you trim the grass.
wrong.why: It can be swallowed or pierce your lip. Put it in the pin cushion.

wrong.text: Run your fingers fast along the grass bundle to smooth it.
wrong.why: Grass edges cut skin. Handle the bundle gently.

wrong.text: Leave the threaded needle stuck in your seat cushion.
wrong.why: Someone will sit on it. Use the pin cushion.

wrong.text: Pull the stitch towards your eye to see if it has seated.
wrong.why: The needle can jerk free. Pull away from your face.

wrong.text: Bite the raffia to cut it when the scissors are across the room.

wrong.text: Point the scissors at a neighbour when passing them over.
wrong.why: Pass scissors closed, handles first.

distractors.name: Rapping iron

distractors.why: They cut thick cane. Grass and raffia are cut with scissors.

distractors.why: Dried grass and raffia do not need a cane trough for this job.

decisions.prompt: The base is starting to cup upwards like a bowl. What is the best response?

options.text: Ease the stitches so that the base lies flat
options.consequence: The base stays flat and the basket stands level.

options.text: Pull every stitch tighter to control it
options.consequence: Tight stitching is what makes the base cup up.

options.text: Press it flat under a weight and carry on as before
options.consequence: It springs back, because the stitch tension has not changed.

decisions.prompt: The grass bundle is getting thinner as you stitch. What do you do?

options.text: Feed in more grass and pass it through the gauge
options.consequence: The coil stays 1 cm thick and the spiral stays flat and regular.

options.text: Carry on, and the coil will even itself out
options.consequence: The thin part makes a dip in the spiral, and the wall looks uneven.

options.text: Fill the thin part later with glue and extra raffia
options.consequence: Glue shows, and the coil is still uneven under it.

decisions.prompt: Your raffia is running out in the middle of a round. How do you add more?

options.text: Splice new raffia under the wrapping so it is hidden
options.consequence: The stitching looks continuous and the join holds.

options.text: Knot the new piece on where it will be seen
options.consequence: Knots on the surface are splices that show, and they lose finishing marks.

options.text: Leave a gap and begin again one stitch later
options.consequence: The gap is a weak spot, and it looks careless.

options.text: Place the next coil on top of the previous round
options.consequence: The wall rises straight up from the edge of the base.

options.text: Set the coil beside the last round, as before
options.consequence: That only makes the base wider, and no side forms.

options.text: Start a separate coil and sew it on later
options.consequence: The join is weak, and the wall will not line up with the base.

observations.prompt: Your spiral has bumps at intervals. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The core was fed unevenly

options.why: Colour changes do not alter the shape.

options.text: The stitches were evenly spaced
options.why: Even stitches give an even surface.

options.text: The base was too flat
options.why: A flat base is what you want.

observations.prompt: Which base shows good coiling?

options.text: A flat, regular spiral with evenly spaced stitches
A bowl-shaped base with tight stitches pulling inwards
options.why: Tension has made it cup up.

options.text: A base with a visible knot at every new length
options.why: Splices should be hidden.

options.text: A spiral that changes from thick to thin at each round
options.why: The core thickness should be constant.

numerics.prompt: A flat coiled base is {d} cm across, and the coil is 1 cm thick. How many rounds does it need?
numerics.working: Radius = {d} ÷ 2 = {answer} cm. At 1 cm per round, that is {answer} rounds.

numerics.prompt: The sides are {d} cm across and {h} cm high, and the coil is 1 cm thick. Taking pi as 3.14, how much core do the sides need, in cm?
numerics.working: One round = 3.14 × {d} cm. A height of {h} cm means {h} rounds. Core = 3.14 × {d} × {h} = {answer} cm.

numerics.prompt: A flat base has {n} rounds of a 1 cm coil, so the mean diameters add up to {n} × {n} cm. Taking pi as 3.14, what length of core does the base need, in cm?
numerics.working: Sum of mean diameters = {n} × {n}. Core = 3.14 × {n} × {n} = {answer} cm.

faults.scenario: Ngozi's coiled basket was meant to have a flat 20 cm base. It rocks on the table and looks rough. Here is what she did.

correct: Keep the bodkin point away from the hand that steadies the base.

wrong.text: Lean close over the upright stakes to look at your weaving.

wrong.text: Cut the cane ends towards your face so that you can see them.
wrong.why: Cut at an angle, away from your face.

wrong.text: Leave the wet floor by the soaking trough for someone else to dry.
wrong.why: A wet floor causes slips. Wipe it up.

wrong.text: Rest the bodkin point against your thigh as you push it in.

wrong.text: Let a long stake spring back without holding it.

wrong.why: A loose blade is easily dropped on your fingers. Use a sharpener.

wrong.text: Lean close over the paper in dim light for hours.
wrong.why: It strains your eyes and back. Sit up, and work in good light.

wrong.text: Draw with your laptop on your lap with its vents blocked, in a dusty corner.
wrong.why: Blocked vents overheat it. Use a flat desk.

wrong.text: Leave drawing boards on the floor between the desks.
wrong.why: People trip over them. Stack them against the wall.

distractors.why: This is a drawing job.

decisions.prompt: The brief is a shopping basket. What do you settle first?

options.text: The user, function, size, materials and cost limit
options.consequence: Everything you draw now answers the brief.

options.text: The colours and the pattern that you most enjoy working with
options.consequence: Colour comes later. It does not answer function.

options.text: The pattern you did last term
options.consequence: The brief may need something different.

decisions.prompt: Your first idea looks good. How many more ideas do you develop?

options.text: At least two more, from observation, memory or imagination
options.consequence: Your preparatory work shows how the idea developed, which earns marks.

options.text: None: a good first idea should go straight to the working drawing
options.consequence: One sketch shows no development, so marks are lost.

options.text: Ten near-copies of the first sketch
options.consequence: Copies do not show a real development of ideas.

decisions.prompt: Your chosen shopping basket has no handle. What do you do?

options.text: Add a strong handle and check that it can be gripped
options.consequence: The article now meets its function.

options.text: Keep it, because a handle spoils the shape
options.consequence: It fails the brief: a shopping basket must be carried.

options.text: Add a thin handle just for looks
options.consequence: A weak handle fails in use, so it does not meet the need.

decisions.prompt: You begin the working drawing. What must it show?

options.text: Elevation and plan with dimensions, and the stated scale
options.consequence: Quantities and making can now be worked out correctly.

options.text: A coloured picture of the basket with no sizes
options.consequence: A picture cannot be used to work out materials.

options.text: The plan only, as the height can be guessed
options.consequence: Height is needed to calculate the stakes.

observations.prompt: Why does a clear working drawing help the later work?

options.text: It makes the calculations and making accurate
It removes any need to measure during the making
options.why: You still measure while making.

options.text: It means that the materials list can be left out of the folio
options.why: The list is still needed.

options.text: It makes the basket lighter
options.why: A drawing cannot change weight.

observations.prompt: You sketch an old market basket that is on your desk. This is drawing from

options.text: Observation
Memory
options.why: You can see it, so you are not relying on memory.

options.text: Imagination
options.why: It already exists in front of you.

options.text: A computer
options.why: No software is being used.

faults.scenario: Sade's preparatory folio earned few of the 20 marks. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She drew one idea only and went straight to making.
lines.why: Ideas must be developed. At least three are expected.

lines.text: She did not list the materials or their quantities.
lines.why: A material list is a required part of the folio.

lines.text: She gave no scale on the working drawing.
lines.why: The scale must be stated.

lines.text: She chose an idea and gave reasons.
lines.why: That is what the brief asks for.

lines.text: She made a day-by-day plan for the five days.
lines.why: That is good planning.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for producing a working drawing.
written.explainPrompt: Why do the preparatory sketches and notes matter in this exam?
written.explainGuide: They carry 20 marks. They show how the idea developed and that the design meets the brief, and a good working drawing makes the material calculations and making accurate.

correct: Sweep up loose fibres and offcuts before any flame is lit.
Tie back long hair and loose clothing before you use a flame.

wrong.text: Singe the basket on the bench among trimmed raffia ends.
wrong.why: Loose fibres catch fire fast. Work outdoors in a clear space with water nearby.

wrong.text: Light the candle next to the open varnish tin to save walking.
wrong.why: Varnish and solvents catch fire. Keep flames well away.

wrong.text: Spray the paint inside the closed store to keep the wind off it.
wrong.why: Fumes build up and can catch fire. Spray only where there is good ventilation.

wrong.text: Hold the flame still on one spot for a darker brown.
wrong.why: The strand burns through, and fire can take hold. Keep the flame moving.

wrong.text: Pour water on a blow lamp to cool it down quickly.
wrong.why: Follow your teacher's instructions for shutting it off, and let it cool in a safe place.

wrong.text: Skip the mask because you will only spray for a short time.
wrong.why: Even a short spray fills the air with fine droplets. Wear the mask.

distractors.name: Rapping iron
distractors.why: The weaving is finished, so there is nothing left to pack.

distractors.name: Soaking trough
distractors.why: Wetting a finished basket would stop the varnish taking.

distractors.name: Tapestry frame
distractors.why: The basket is already made.

distractors.name: Household kerosene
distractors.why: It is a dangerous fire risk near a flame, and it is not a finish.

distractors.name: Dye pot
distractors.why: Colour here is scorched or sprayed on, not dyed.

distractors.name: Thick floor paint
distractors.why: It clogs the weave. Use thin coats of the listed finish.

decisions.prompt: Fluffy fibres stand out over the basket. How do you use the flame?

options.text: One quick pass, keeping the flame moving
options.consequence: The fluff goes and the strands are unharmed.

options.text: Hold the flame close until the area turns dark
options.consequence: You burn into the strands and damage them.

options.text: Go over it again and again to be thorough
options.consequence: Repeated heat scorches the strands and may set them alight.

decisions.prompt: You have just sanded the rough areas. What comes before the varnish?

options.text: Brush off all the dust
options.consequence: The varnish goes on clean and clear.

options.text: Varnish at once while the surface is fresh
options.consequence: The varnish traps dust and dries rough.

options.text: Wet the basket and varnish it while it is damp
options.consequence: Varnish does not take evenly on a wet surface.

decisions.prompt: You want a strong finish. How do you apply the varnish?

options.text: Thin coats, letting each dry before the next
options.consequence: Thin coats dry clear and hard.

options.text: One very thick coat to save time
options.consequence: Thick coats run and stay tacky.

options.text: Second coat straight on the wet first coat
options.consequence: It stays tacky, with runs.

decisions.prompt: The rim has sharp cut ends after trimming. What do you do?

options.text: Bind or wrap it neatly with cane or raffia
options.consequence: It makes a smooth, strong border that will not catch on hands.

options.text: Leave them, as varnish will cover them
options.consequence: Varnish does not cover sharp ends, and they can scratch the user.

options.text: Burn them off with the flame
options.consequence: That can scorch the rim and start a fire.

observations.prompt: What happens to a thin coat of varnish?

options.text: It dries clear
It runs and stays tacky
options.why: That is a thick coat.

options.text: It stays white
options.why: Clear varnish does not stay white.

options.text: It peels off straight away
options.why: That is not expected.

observations.prompt: Light scorching, moved steadily across the cane, gives

options.text: Graded brown tones
Bright red colour
options.why: Scorching browns the surface.

options.text: A shiny varnish finish
options.why: That comes from varnish.

options.text: No change at all
options.why: Heat browns cane.

faults.scenario: Ada's basket finished sticky, with burn marks. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She held the flame on each spot to get rid of the fluff.
lines.why: Holding the flame still burns the strands. Keep it moving.

lines.text: She brushed on one thick coat of varnish.
lines.why: Thick coats run and stay tacky.

lines.text: She varnished a basket that was still dusty from sanding.
lines.why: Dust gets trapped in the varnish.

lines.text: She kept water nearby while using the flame.
lines.why: That is correct safety practice.

lines.text: She varnished the inside as well as the outside.
lines.why: That is what the job calls for.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for singeing and varnishing a basket.
written.explainPrompt: Why are two thin coats of varnish better than one thick coat?
written.explainGuide: Thin coats dry clear and hard. A thick coat runs and stays tacky, and the surface dries before the inside does. A second thin coat then builds up an even finish.

correct: Keep your receipts in one file so that no cost is lost.
Sit upright at the desk and rest your eyes between long calculations.

wrong.text: Leave the workshop cash box open on the bench while you add up.
wrong.why: Money can go missing. Lock it away.

wrong.text: Throw away the receipts as soon as you have paid.
wrong.why: Receipts are the record of your costs. Keep them.

wrong.text: Work out prices in your head and write nothing down.
wrong.why: Costs get lost. Record every cost.

wrong.text: Write costs on loose scraps of paper.
wrong.why: Scraps get lost. Use the record book.

wrong.text: Use last year's material prices so you need not check.
wrong.why: Prices change, so the cost will be wrong. Review them.

decisions.prompt: The monthly workshop rent is on your list. How do you class it?

options.text: As a fixed cost, shared across the month's output
options.consequence: It is charged fairly across all the baskets.

options.text: As a variable cost for this batch only
options.consequence: Rent does not change with output, so that is the wrong class.

options.text: Leave it out, because it is not about baskets
options.consequence: You lose money every month on unrecorded rent.

decisions.prompt: Fixed costs are N12,000 a month for 24 baskets. Your batch is 10. What do you charge?

options.consequence: The batch pays its fair share of the month.

options.text: The full N12,000 to this batch
options.consequence: The price comes out too high, because other baskets also share it.

options.text: Nothing, as it is already paid
options.consequence: Prices must recover the fixed costs too.

decisions.prompt: Labour was your own time, so a classmate says to leave it out. What do you do?

options.text: Include it, because your time is a real cost
options.consequence: The unit cost is true, so the price pays you too.

options.text: Leave it out to keep the price low for the buyers
options.consequence: This hides a real cost, and you work for nothing.

options.text: Count only half of it
options.consequence: There is no reason to halve it.

decisions.prompt: Your price comes to N3,000, and a plastic basket sells for N2,000. What do you do?

options.text: Compare quality and demand, then review the price
options.consequence: The price reflects cost, demand, competition and quality.

options.text: Cut it to N1,500 at once, so that you beat the plastic basket
options.consequence: That is below the unit cost, so you make a loss.

options.text: Ignore the competitor altogether
options.consequence: Competition is a factor that decides price.

options.text: It falls, because fixed costs are spread more thinly

options.text: It stays exactly the same
options.why: Unit cost changes because fixed costs are shared.

options.text: It becomes zero
options.why: Costs do not disappear.

Workshop rent

options.why: That does not change with output.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for costing a batch of baskets accurately.
written.explainPrompt: Why does making more baskets a month lower the cost of each basket?
written.explainGuide: Fixed costs such as rent stay the same, so spreading them over more baskets means each one carries a smaller share, and the unit cost falls.
